rationale: Mistastin is one of very few impact structures with anorthosite in the target rocks; south-pole highland units are feldspathic impact materials. Not 1.0: terrestrial plagioclase is more sodic than lunar ferroan anorthosite and the rocks are weathered.
Basin-massif highland material vs anorthosite-bearing impact target. Same caveats on plagioclase composition and alteration.

Ries suevite and impact breccias were used for Apollo-era geology training (impact processes), but the target is sedimentary cover over granitic/gneissic basement, not anorthosite. Site is vegetated and farmed.
Classic shock features (coesite was found here) but the target rocks are sandstone and limestone/dolomite: impact process yes, lunar mineralogy no.
Impact breccias present, but the target is a Paleozoic carbonate sequence over crystalline basement; carbonate mineralogy is non-lunar.
Impact crater in Deccan flood basalt with shocked plagioclase (maskelynite reported): a recognised mare-basalt impact analog. Continental flood basalt is more oxidised and altered than mare basalt.
Young basaltic lava field (NASA field research site); mare-like basalt mineralogy, terrestrial oxidation and weathering.
Hydrothermal salt deposits and hyperacidic brines: no lunar counterpart.
Carbonate (hydromagnesite) lake sediments formed in water; aqueous mineralogy is absent on the Moon. Lake Salda is a Mars (Jezero) analog.
Acidic iron-sulfate (jarosite) system driven by water and microbes; non-lunar.
Dome C is a ~3 km thick ice sheet: no rock exposed to test on.
Dome C is almost flat over 10 km (relief of tens of metres); the Shackleton patch has ~1.6 km relief and ~19 deg mean slope at 500 m.

The 10 km window is mostly the flat plain around the 1.2 km crater (patch relief ~80 m, mean slope <1 deg at 500 m) vs ~500 m relief and ~4 deg on Slater Plain. Crater shape matches, patch statistics do not.
Same simple-bowl shape but ~17x smaller (1.2 km vs ~21 km): the 10 km window is flat plain while the Shackleton patch is steep crater interior (~19 deg mean slope).
Both low-slope, but the plateau has ~3x the relief (~280 m vs ~80 m) and ~4 deg vs <1 deg mean slope at 500 m.
The Haughton 10 km window is low relief (~110 m, ~2 deg): erosion has subdued the 23 km crater, while the Nobile rim patch has ~780 m relief.
Steep glacial valley walls (~1.5 km relief, ~15 deg mean slope at 500 m) vs the steep Haworth crater wall (~2.2 km, ~14 deg): similar steepness, different origin (glacial vs impact).

Closest Earth approach for cold and polar light (winter surface ~190-200 K, months of polar night), but the Shackleton patch is permanent shadow at ~45-110 K. Would mislead cryogenic tests; capped by the PSR rule anyway.

Sunlit massif (mean ~113 K, max ~266 K, almost no PSR): Dome C (~200-250 K surface) overlaps only the warm end of the lunar range, and its noon sun reaches ~38 deg vs <7 deg on the Moon. Near-neutral.
Haworth patch is half permanent shadow (mean ~46 K); the Dry Valleys (mean air ~-20 C) are polar and dry but ~200 K warmer.
Polar day/night and cold, but the lunar site has no polar night, sun below ~9 deg, and mean ~100 K vs ~260 K. Uninformative.
One of the hottest places on Earth with high noon sun; opposite of a polar cold trap.
Tropical site (~20 N): noon sun near zenith, warm monsoon climate, no polar light geometry.
Continuous permafrost with ice-cemented ground on Devon Island (HMP drill tests); Haworth has thermally stable ice within 1 m. Ice temperature (~260 K vs <110 K) and volatile mix differ.
Buried glacier ice under a dry sublimation till: ice preserved under a desiccated cover, conceptually like lunar ice-stability depth. Ice age is debated; temperatures differ by >150 K.
Ice-cemented permafrost below a dry surface layer in a hyperarid cold desert; Cabeus B has ice ~0.2 m deep. Physics of vapour-diffusion-controlled ice is analogous; temperatures are not.
ISRU hardware heritage on tephra (NASA/PISCES field tests) but no ground ice at the saddle; icy simulant has to be emplaced.
Warm sandstone desert with no ground ice vs an ice-rich lunar crater.
Tropical savanna with a wet season and no ground ice vs a cold-trap-dominated patch.
Glass-rich basaltic tephra used in ISRU / regolith field tests (point sites). The 10 km patch also includes wetter, vegetated ground; basaltic (mare-like) rather than anorthositic, no agglutinates.
Cinder and basaltic fines in the San Francisco volcanic field (Desert RATS area; the JSC-1 simulant came from a cinder cone in the same field). Mare-like, not highland; the patch is partly vegetated.
Hyperarid fine dust with near-zero moisture, but oxidised and salt-rich (nitrates, sulfates, perchlorate), unlike lunar regolith.
Moist, organic-rich agricultural soils under vegetation.
Snow and firn surface: no mineral regolith.
Farmland and forest; abundant biology.
Among the driest, lowest-biomass soils on Earth, but not sterile (microbes and organics are detected).
Cold hyperarid desert with very low biomass; soil microbes and endoliths are present.
Tropical savanna woodland.
Ice-sheet surface with very low biomass, but a permanently staffed station adds human-borne contamination.
Hundreds of accessible basaltic lava-tube caves used in planetary cave and robotics analog work; lunar tubes are likely much larger.
La Corona lava tube (several km, partly below sea level), used in ESA astronaut training. Humid, partly flooded, scale smaller than lunar tubes.
Very long basaltic lava-tube system, but humid, vegetated collapse sections and tropical biology.
No lava tubes; hydrothermal salt terrain.
Desert RATS rover/EVA traverse site on a basaltic lava flow and cinder terrain; low-slope plateau-like ground. Check patch slope statistics.
Long-running remote polar rover/EVA analog (HMP), but Haworth's patch is much steeper (~98% of ground >10 deg at 500 m).
Fields, forest, roads and villages: obstacles and surfaces that do not exist on the Moon.
Proven overwintering/isolation operations (ESA uses Concordia for isolation research), but a flat ice surface is nothing like the crater terrain for landing or driving.
